newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Ssangyong aims to post profit by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Ssangyong aims to post profit by 2000.

text.p: South Korean utility vehicle maker Ssangyong Motor Co said on Friday it hopes to be profitable in two to three years by developing innovative models.
"We will do all we can to turn a profit by the year 2000. Development of new models will be an essential part of our pursuits," said Cho Min-kyung, a Ssangyong Motor spokesman.
Ssangyong suffers from snowballing losses as a result of past facility expansions. Its popular utility vehicles are developed with Daimler-Benz AG subsidiary Mercedes-Benz.
Ssangyong is expected to register a net loss of about 130 billion won ($151.95 million) for calendar 1996, after incurring a 126 billion won loss in 1995 and a 79 billion loss in 1994.
The company earlier said it wanted to cut the loss to about 50 billion won this year. It set a 1997 sales target of two trillion won against an estimated 1.38 trillion won in 1996.
The losses have led to rumours that the struggling firm was negotiating to be taken over by Samsung Group, which recently entered the automotive business.
"We will never sell our company to anyone despite rising losses," Cho said.
To help the company return to the black, union workers declared in January that they would accept a wage freeze and give up all negotiation on working conditions until the firm turns a profit.
Part of Ssangyong's strategy will be to differentiate itself through quality and not compete on a mass production basis.
The strategy worked four years ago when Ssangyong rolled out its Musso utility vehicles equipped with engines developed by Mercedes-Benz.
The model was well received by local drivers, whose access to foreign cars is limited by high taxes. In July 1995, Ssangyong rolled out Istana vans, also built with Mercedes technology.
Ssangyong will also develop new models in cooperation with foreign partners.
In October, the company plans to market new luxury sedans developed with assistance from Mercedes-Benz.
Annual production for sedans with an engine capacity of 3.2 litres would be about 30,000 units per year, of which 50 percent would be for export, it said.
"No carmakers in the country have ever tried to export large-sized sedans in such scale. We expect it to be a hit with domestic and overseas customers as well," Cho said.
The company plans to increase yearly passenger car production to 200,000 units by 2000.
Ssangyong also will produce 250,000 four-wheel drive utility vehicles and 130,000 vans and light commercial vehicles by then, he said.
Ssangyong, which is 3.62 percent owned by Mercedes-Benz, said it would seek technical help from the German company to develop an export model aimed at marketing in Asia, he said.
